summary: Galbraith treats organizational design as a problem of information processing: the more uncertain the task, the more information must flow during execution. arguments: Task uncertainty drives the information-processing load a structure must carry.
Rules, hierarchy and goals handle routine coordination; exceptions overload them.
Design options either reduce information needs or increase processing capacity, and each has costs.

generalizability: High for coordination-heavy units such as a department that links scouting, analytics, coaching and the front office.
relevance: A strategic coordination department is, by definition, a lateral information-processing mechanism; this explains when it is worth its cost.

title: The Concept of Information Overload: A Review of Literature from Organization Science, Accounting, Marketing, MIS, and Related Disciplines
summary: A cross-disciplinary literature review of information overload: its definitions, causes, symptoms and countermeasures. It describes a recurring finding that decision performance rises with information up to a point and then declines.
arguments: Beyond a point, more information lowers decision quality.
Causes include the information itself, the task, the person, the organization and technology.
Countermeasures include filtering, structuring, better formats and changed processes.
design: Narrative literature review across several management disciplines.
strengths: Broad synthesis with a usable framework of causes and remedies.
limitations: Review of heterogeneous studies; the inverted-U pattern is a summary, not a precise estimate.
generalizability: High for report and meeting design.
relevance: Explains why a 22-page report can be worse than a two-page brief.
